writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The government is committed to protecting consumers across the UK, including in Scotland, from subscription traps. The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 introduces new protections to give consumers greater transparency and control over subscription contracts. These include clearer information before entering a contract, reminders before certain renewal payments, cooling-off rights, and straightforward arrangements for cancelling subscriptions. We anticipate these measures will provide £436 million of consumer benefit per year.

Subject to Parliamentary approval, the new regime will come into force on 1 January 2027. Guidance has also been produced to help businesses prepare for and comply with the new requirements.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, whether the Government Digital Service holds a record of the AI models used by government departments.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
There is currently no central tracking of use of models within government, but there is a relevant initiative focused on algorithmic transparency and some further planned activity in the Cabinet Office.

For tools that have a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect, or directly interact with the public, government publishes information via the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS). The ATRS captures comprehensive information about algorithmic tools, including about the models they are built on, their design, purpose, governance, and role in decision-making. Publication of records is mandatory for central government and arm's length bodies that deliver front line services, and it is recommended best practice for the wider public sector.

ATRS records are published on GOV.UK. At time of writing, 157 records have been published since the Standard was first launched in 2021. These come from a wide variety of government departments and agencies, with more being added every month. HMG departments are required to identify and produce records for all tools that fall in scope of the ATRS. The Government Digital Service regularly check with departments to ensure that this is on track.

This approach aims to deliver meaningful transparency, where the general public can access high-level explanations quickly and easily, and specialised or interested parties can explore more detailed information as they wish.

The Cabinet Office Future Civil Service team are looking to create a centralised view on AI deployment across departments. The recently established the GovAI Unit within the Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, will coordinate, develop and scale AI solutions across Government in collaboration with the Prime Minister’s AI Taskforce. The Government is committed to the ethical and transparent deployment of AI with appropriate guardrails, as our overriding principle.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what assessment her Department has made of trends in the level of teacher recruitment and retention challenges in specialist subjects, including modern foreign languages, music and digital skills, ahead of the implementation of the reformed Key Stage 3 curriculum.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department recognises the value of strong teachers working in every classroom across key stage 3 and key stage 4. That is why we have recruited more than 3,000 new secondary teachers, continue to invest in initial teacher training and have set out plans through the Schools White Paper for a Teacher Training Entitlement, so that every teacher can access high-quality professional development.

Our schoolteacher pipeline is also growing, with nearly 32,600 new entrants to Initial Teacher Training (ITT) in Autumn 2025, up 13% from the previous year. There were 17,200 entrants to secondary postgraduate ITT (PGITT) courses in the 2025/26 academic year, 1,900 more than in the 2024/25 academic year.

Modern foreign languages had 1,378 PGITT entrants in 2025/26, compared with 1,179 in 2024/25, which is a 17% increase.

Music had 369 PGITT entrants in 2025/26, compared with 345 in 2024/25, which is a 7% increase.

Computing had 723 PGITT entrants in 2025/26, a 46% increase on 2024/25. This is the highest number of computing PGITT entrants since comparable statistics began in 2012/13.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government whether participation in the proposed education technology (EdTech) certification scheme will be mandatory or voluntary for suppliers of EdTech products.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department launched its consultation on the proposed education technology and artificial intelligence product safety certification scheme on 10 November 2026. Under the proposals set out for consultation, the certification scheme would not initially be mandatory. The department does not currently have specific powers to require suppliers to obtain certification or education settings to use certified products.

The department proposes instead to set a clear expectation through statutory guidance that education settings should obtain proportionate assurance that products within the scheme’s scope meet the relevant safety standards. Certification would ordinarily provide that assurance, while allowing settings to rely on equivalent evidence where this is justified. The consultation also seeks views on whether legislative underpinning may be needed in future.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government whether the standards assessed by the proposed education technology certification scheme will include (1) children’s physical and mental health implications, (2) data privacy implications, and (3) superiority of learning outcomes.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department launched its consultation on the proposed education technology and artificial intelligence product safety certification scheme on 10 November 2026. Under the proposals set out for consultation, products would be assessed against a range of criteria including data privacy, and children’s mental health and cognitive, social and emotional development. The consultation also seeks views on whether there are additional risks that the scheme proposal currently does not cover.

Physical health is not proposed as a separate certification criterion and certification would not assess a product’s overall educational effectiveness, except where a lack of effectiveness could put children at risk of harm.

The department will continue to support settings to make evidence-informed decisions about product effectiveness through guidance and evidence on what works, including the EdTech Testbed programme in partnership with the Education Endowment Foundation.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, what assessment he has made of the potential merits of expanding access to digital assistive technologies for neurodiverse individuals entering employment.

writtenQuestions.answerText:

This approach can include the use of accessible digital technologies to enable independence and greater inclusion and participation for people who face barriers to employment due to health and disability, including neurodivergent people. Stakeholders advise that a range of assistive technology already exists in mainstream devices, software, and IT platforms, but users are not aware of it or can struggle to use it. We want to work with industry leaders to ensure that employers and disabled employees can make the most of this technology.

My right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions has so far hosted two roundtables with big tech companies and leading UK disability charities to identify practical ways that cutting-edge technology can remove barriers preventing disabled and neurodivergent people from finding and keeping jobs.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, whether his Department collects data on the employment outcomes of workers made redundant from technology and digital occupations, including (a) the average length of time before securing new employment and (b) changes in earnings following re-employment; and what support his Department provides to such workers who remain unemployed six months after redundancy.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Work and Pensions
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Department for Work and Pensions monitors data published by the independent Office for National Statistics on the estimated number of redundancies by industry. Such industries include ‘Information & communication’ and ‘Professional, Scientific & Technical Activities’. This data may be accessed using this link: RED02: Redundancies by age, industry and region - Office for National Statistics

The Department provides support to employers and individuals affected by redundancy through its Rapid Response Service. The service aims to help people move quickly into alternative employment and can provide tailored support including help with job search and CVs, identifying transferable skills, accessing appropriate training and overcoming barriers to securing new employment. Support can begin when an individual is under threat of redundancy or during their notice period and can normally continue for up to 13 weeks following redundancy, whether or not the individual makes a claim to benefit.

The Department also reviews published data on the duration of Universal Credit (UC) claims, and the rate at which UC customers in the ‘searching for work’ conditionality regime enter employment. writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, (a) what standards will govern the inclusion or exclusion of detailed psychotherapy and psychological therapy session notes relating to children in the Single Patient Record and (b) what assessment has been made of whether existing shared care records apply equivalent safeguards.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
In respect of the Single Patient Record, discussions are ongoing on a range of practical issues about its scope and operation, and that includes determining what arrangements should apply to the sharing of psychotherapy and psychological therapy records, including the highly personal and private information contained in the notes of therapy sessions.

No final decisions have been made in this area, and we are extremely mindful of the views of patient groups, therapy professionals and other stakeholders, and of the debates that have previously taken place in other contexts about the need to prevent inappropriate third party access to confidential therapy notes. We will provide further updates in due course.

More generally, the controllers of a shared care record are required under the common law duty of confidentiality to communicate adequately to their local communities the existence and purposes of a shared care record, its impact on individuals and their right to object to some or all of their confidential patient information being included within that shared record.

Furthermore, the controllers of the shared care record must also ensure that they comply with UK General Data Protection Regulation requirements that data is processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently, making reasonable efforts to ensure that individuals are informed about how their personal data is used.

In accordance with s251B of the Health and Social Care Act 2012, it is appropriate for clinicians to share information through a shared care record with other clinicians responsible for a patient’s care, unless that patient objects, or it is reasonable for them to believe that the patient would object. When it is necessary for direct care purposes, for example in an emergency situation, and those purposes are consistent with the reasonable expectations of the individual patient, health professionals will also rely on an assumption of consent to share essential information with other professionals responsible for the patient’s care.

However, as with all health records, there are strict rules and guidance in place to prevent unauthorised, inappropriate and unjustifiable access to confidential patient information by NHS employees, regardless of whether that information is held on a shared record, with staff who breach those rules facing suspension, dismissal and potential prosecution.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask His Majesty's Government what plans they have, if any, to amend the Care Quality Commission's inspection framework or introduce legislative changes where appropriate, to ensure that cyber resilience is assessed as part of health and social care providers' responsibilities for safe care, operational continuity, governance and the protection of people's information.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) is a self-assessment toolkit that must be completed by health and social care providers to access National Health Service data. The DSPT’s requirements include a minimum data security training requirement for staff, organisational policies governing the use of personal devices, and the management of unsupported systems.

To support social care providers in strengthening their cyber security and resilience, the Department established the Better Security, Better Care (BSBC) programme in 2021. writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
This Government recognises that technology can create new opportunities for perpetrators of VAWG, and we are committed to preventing and tackling abuse that occurs online.

In January 2024, the Online Safety Act introduced a threatening communications offence, which criminalised sending communications that threaten death, serious injury, and rape, where the sender intends for the recipient to fear that the threat will be carried out.

The Act requires also requires in-scope platforms, including social media platforms, to proactively tackle harmful and illegal content online. This includes proactively removing content that constitutes harassment, fear or provocation of violence, and sexual exploitation, all of which are priority offences.

The Home Office is investing in a pilot network of covert online officers to improve capabilities in identifying and targeting the most technologically sophisticated VAWG offenders. Insights gained from the pilot will be shared with Ofcom to help address the use of online platforms to cause harm.

We have robust legislation in place to deal with threatening, abusive or harassing behaviour and the stirring up of racial and religious hatred. This includes communications offences under the Malicious Communications Act 1988 and Communications Act 2003, and the false and threatening communications offences in the Online Safety Act 2023.

Hate crime is also designated as a priority offence under the Online Safety Act 2023. Online services must take proactive steps to prevent their services being used to facilitate or commit such offences and have systems and processes in place to tackle illegal content.

The Government has increased funding to the police National Online Hate Crime Hub, providing £1.6 million per year to increase and improve the investigative capability of the police to tackle online hate. It also funds True Vision, which enables victims to report hate crime online.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what recent assessment she has made of the adequacy of the Unsafe Journey Policy; and whether she has made an assessment of the potential merits of waiving biometric requirements for families in Gaza.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Home Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Biometric enrolment (in the form of facial images and fingerprints) underpins identity assurance, national and border security, and the integrity of the immigration system. It enables checks against immigration and criminality records to identify individuals who may pose a threat to national security, public safety or immigration controls. It also supports safeguarding, particularly of children, by helping to verify applicants’ identities and reduce the risk of identity fraud and exploitation.

Given the strong public interest in biometric checks, deferring or excusing enrolment before arrival in the UK must remain an exceptional step.

The Government keeps all of its policies, including the Unsafe Journeys Policy, under review. This ensures that it appropriately balances the circumstances of vulnerable applicants with the need to secure the UK borders and maintain effective immigration control. The Unsafe Journeys policy was last updated in March 2026.

The Government recognises the exceptionally difficult circumstances facing families in Gaza. Requests for biometric deferral and excusal are considered on a case-by-case basis, taking account of individual circumstances and relevant human rights obligations.

The existing policy provides a mechanism for considering exceptional circumstances while maintaining these essential safeguards.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what steps he is taking to ensure that the armed forces are prepared for any attack on a NATO country.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Defence
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The UK’s commitment to NATO is unwavering. NATO is a defensive Alliance: we do not seek conflict, but we are clear that we will defend every inch of Allied territory. Our NATO-first approach puts the Alliance at the heart of how we organise, equip and train our Armed Forces, driving improvements in warfighting readiness and ensuring the UK can play its full part in defending the Alliance. That commitment is backed by forces on the ground today, including through our leadership of NATO’s Forward Land Forces in Estonia, alongside our wider land, air and maritime contributions across the Alliance.

We are sustaining this readiness through an ambitious programme of training and exercising with NATO across all domains, from the North Atlantic and High North to NATO’s eastern flank. Our forces train routinely with Allies to strengthen interoperability and practise their ability to reinforce, deploy, integrate and sustain combat power in crisis and conflict. In 2027, the UK will make a major contribution to STEADFAST DEFENDER, NATO’s principal live collective defence exercise. UK-led exercises and activity across multiple domains will test our ability to reinforce Allies, project forces across Europe and sustain combat power at scale as part of NATO’s warfighting plans.

We are backing this with nearly £300 billion of investment in our Armed Forces over the next four years through the Defence Investment Plan, including £15 billion in additional spending power. NATO is at the heart of the Plan, ensuring our investment prioritises the forces and capabilities needed to strengthen UK warfighting readiness and deliver the Alliance’s warfighting plans.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, with reference to the consultation outcome, Home buying and selling reform roadmap, updated 19 June 2026, how will the property condition report differ from the home condition report previously required under home information packs.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
This government recognises that previous attempts to reform the home buying and selling process did not succeed.

Home Information Packs were criticised for adding cost, relying on jargon and failing to give buyers the information they needed. They were paper-based and introduced without sufficient industry collaboration.

Our approach has been co-developed with industry and will be phased in gradually, building on work to digitalise the home moving process. Sales packs will include property searches and a property condition report, giving buyers important information before they make an offer. The information underpinning sales packs will come from trusted data sources, with clear standards and the ability to update as needed.

We will work with industry to agree the final detail of what should be included in sales packs ahead of legislation.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, whether she plans to introduce an automatic escalation mechanism where park home site owners repeatedly fail to comply with site licence conditions.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Existing site licensing legislation, namely the Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960, the Mobile Homes Act 2013, and the Mobile Homes (Requirement for Manager of Site to be Fit and Proper Person) (England) Regulations 2020, give local authorities substantial powers over residential park home sites.

When considering planning applications, local authorities are expected to take account of flood risk and the emergency arrangements in place to protect residents. Before issuing a site licence, they must also consider matters including the arrangements for funding and managing the site and the proposed site licence holder’s ability to comply with licence conditions and provide for its long-term maintenance.

Local authorities must also assess whether the person managing the site is fit and proper, having regard to their conduct and competence. Once a site licence has been granted, we expect local authorities to monitor sites and take early enforcement where planning or site licencing conditions are breached. writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer, what steps his Department is taking to support the development and implementation of the UK’s regulatory framework for digital assets.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Treasury
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government’s ambition is for the UK to become the global destination of choice for next-generation financial markets by 2030, while maintaining appropriate standards of consumer protection and market integrity.

As set out at Mansion House 2026, HM Treasury is supporting the development and implementation of the UK’s regulatory framework for digital assets through a comprehensive programme of work, working alongside the Bank of England, Financial Conduct Authority and industry. This work has three strategic pillars: cryptoassets and stablecoins, next-generation payments, and the digitalisation of wholesale financial markets.

On cryptoassets, we have established a comprehensive regulatory regime, including stablecoins, due to take effect from October 2027.

On Payments, the Financial Services and Markets Bill currently before Parliament seeks to give the Bank of England a secondary innovation objective in relation to its regulation of systemic payment systems and digital settlement asset service providers. This will support the Government's aim for the UK to remain at the forefront of innovation in payments and digital finance.

On wholesale markets, our focus is on moving from experimentation to wider adoption. The Digital Securities Sandbox (DSS) provides a modified regulatory environment in which firms can undertake live digital-asset activity. Seventeen firms have entered the Sandbox, with three firms authorised to conduct live activity and further authorisations expected. The Government has also tabled an amendment to the Financial Services and Markets Bill that would allow HM Treasury to update specified legislation to reflect technological change in financial market infrastructure and support the adoption and scaling of digital assets and tokenised markets.

We are also supporting the development of the wider market infrastructure needed for adoption, including working towards delivering the pilot of the Digital Gilt Instrument (DIGIT), which is set to take place by Q1 2027. The government appointed Christopher Woolard CBE as Wholesale Digital Markets Champion. His first report, published in July 2026 sets out priorities and recommendations for developing the UK’s tokenised wholesale markets which are now being taken forward.

writtenStatements.title: UK National Risk Assessment of Proliferation Financing
writtenStatements.text:
My right honourable friend the Economic Secretary to the Treasury (Lucy Rigby) has today made the following statement:

The proliferation of chemical, biological and nuclear weapons poses a serious and evolving threat to the United Kingdom's national security and to the wider international community. Proliferation financing (PF) remains central to the ability of hostile states and networks to procure materials, technology and expertise in support of illicit weapons programmes.

As a global financial centre and trading hub, the UK is exposed to indirect and inherent PF risks. This updated National Risk Assessment of Proliferation Financing (PF NRA), published on 23 November 2026, sets out the Government's assessment of those threats and vulnerabilities, building on the UK's first PF NRA published in 2021. The publication fulfils the requirement under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 (the MLRs) to maintain an up-to-date assessment of UK proliferation financing risks.

Produced by HM Treasury, with contributions from across government, supervisors, law enforcement and academic experts, the assessment provides an updated and evidence-based overview of the proliferation financing risks facing the UK. It reflects significant developments since 2021, including the increasing sophistication of sanctions evasion and procurement networks, the growing use of cryptoassets and cyber-enabled activity, and enhancements to the UK's counter-proliferation financing framework.

The key findings of the PF NRA are:

  1. The UK’s financial sector remains at high risk from proliferators. The assessment concludes that the UK's proliferation financing risk remains largely indirect and inadvertent, principally arising from the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) and Iran-linked procurement and financing networks. The UK's position as a major international financial, trading and shipping centre means that legitimate financial and commercial activity may be exploited by proliferators seeking to generate revenue, procure goods and technology, or evade sanctions. The assessment finds that banking and payments, trade finance providers, insurers, legal and professional service providers, and virtual asset service providers remain particularly exposed to proliferation financing risks. It also highlights emerging threats, including the use of cryptoassets, cyber-enabled activity and DPRK-linked remote IT workers to generate revenue and evade sanctions.
  2. The DPRK and Iran remain the most significant proliferation financing actors at state level. Both continue to rely on procurement and financing networks to evade sanctions, generate revenue and acquire goods, technology and expertise in support of their weapons programmes.
  3. Despite these threats, the 2026 assessment finds that the UK has continued to strengthen its strategic, regulatory and operational capabilities to counter proliferation financing. This includes updating relevant sanctions regimes, introducing new export controls and corporate transparency measures, and requiring firms regulated under the MLRs to identify, assess and mitigate PF risk. Together, these measures enhance the UK’s ability to detect, prevent and disrupt proliferation financing activity, while supporting firms, as the first line of defence, to apply proportionate and risk-based controls.

The report is available at: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-risk-assessment-of-proliferation-financing-2026

This updated PF NRA demonstrates the UK's continued commitment to countering proliferation financing and protecting the integrity of the UK’s financial system. Since the publication of the first PF NRA in 2021, the UK has strengthened its counter-proliferation financing framework through enhancements to sanctions implementation and enforcement, export controls, corporate transparency and regulatory requirements on firms. The assessment supports the UK's wider national security objectives and reflects our continued leadership in international efforts to improve understanding of PF risks and strengthen implementation of Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards.

The assessment supports the UK's wider national security objectives and reflects our continued leadership in international efforts to improve understanding of PF risks and strengthen implementation of Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards.
